title: Med Spa Cancellation Policy: Template, Fees and No-Show Rules
summary: Med spa cancellation policy template with notice windows and fees by service tier, per-visit vs per-service fee rules, late arrivals and dispute records.
body_markdown:
## What a Med Spa Cancellation Policy Has to Decide


A med spa cancellation policy has to settle six things: how much notice counts as on time, what a late cancellation costs, what a no-show costs, when a late arrival becomes a no-show, who can waive a fee, and how the patient agreed to all of it. A policy that only covers the first two leaves the front desk improvising on the rest.


The guides that rank for this topic cover notice periods and fee amounts well.[PatientNow's cancellation policy article](https://www.patientnow.com/resources/blog/appointment-cancellation-policy) walks through notice periods, exceptions and staff scripts.[Pabau's cancellation policy guide](https://pabau.com/blog/med-spa-cancellation-policy-guide/) adds a fee matrix by treatment. None of them deal with what happens when the written policy and the booking software disagree, which is where the clinics that contact us actually get stuck.


If your real goal is fewer missed visits, start with our guide on[how to reduce med spa no-shows](https://decodahealth.com/blog/how-to-reduce-med-spa-no-shows) , which covers reminder timing and the research behind it. This post is about the rulebook itself.


## Notice Windows and Fees by Service Tier


Set the notice window by how hard the slot is to refill, and the fee by what the empty slot costs. PatientNow describes at least 24 hours as typical, with some med spas asking 48 hours for longer or pricier services, and Pabau gives the same 24 to 48 hour range. A 20-minute neurotoxin visit can be refilled from a waitlist the same morning. A two-hour laser block usually cannot.


The table below is a starting point, not survey data. It follows the same ticket tiers we use in the no-show guide, so the two stay consistent. Adjust the numbers to your own prices and how quickly your waitlist fills openings.


Service tier Notice window Held at booking Late cancellation No-show


Free or low-cost consults (under about $150) 24 hours Nothing, or card on file No fee; warn on repeat Card or prepayment required to rebook


Injectables and facials (about $150 to $400) 24 hours Card on file Flat fee or 50% of the booked service Higher flat fee or the full service price


Laser, body contouring, full-face filler ($400 and up) 48 hours Deposit of 20% to 50%, credited to treatment Deposit kept Deposit kept; prepay to rebook


Prepaid package or membership visit Same as the service The session itself Fee, or session kept with a warning Session forfeited or fee charged, as written in the package terms


Package and membership visits need their own line because the patient has already paid. Decide whether a missed prepaid session is forfeited or charged a fee, and write that into the package terms next to your[med spa package refund policy](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-package-refund-policy) .


## Per-Visit or Per-Service: The Fee Math That Surprises Front Desks


Decide whether the fee applies once per visit or once per booked service, and put that in writing. Booking software often attaches the fee to the service, so a patient who stacks treatments can owe several fees for one missed visit.


Two clinics raised this with us. One owner asked whether a patient with three stacked services, each carrying a fixed fee, would pay one fee or three. At another, the front desk expected a flat $100 no-show fee. The patient had booked two services with a $250 fee on each, and the charge came to $500. The written policy said per visit. The setup said per service.


Neither approach is wrong. A per-service fee makes sense when each treatment ties up a different provider or device. A per-visit fee is simpler to explain at the desk and easier to defend when a patient objects. What matters is that the number on the policy page matches the number the system produces. Test it by booking a multi-service visit as a patient and cancelling it late.


## Late Arrivals: When a Late Patient Becomes a No-Show


Write a grace period into the policy and say what happens after it. Published policies and vendor guides usually set it at 10 to 15 minutes; Pabau's guide uses 15. After that, the provider decides whether to shorten the treatment, rebook it, or count the visit as missed.


The harder case is the patient who arrives after the no-show is recorded. One front desk lead told us patients show up 30 to 60 minutes late, the provider agrees to see them, and staff then need to undo a status that has already triggered a fee. Your policy should say who can reverse a no-show and that the reversal is logged with a reason. Otherwise every late arrival becomes an argument at the desk.


Chronic lateness is often a scheduling problem. If providers routinely run behind, patients learn that arriving late is safe, so fix your[buffer time between med spa appointments](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-appointment-buffer-time) before you tighten the grace period.


## Your Reminder Texts Can Contradict Your Policy


A reminder that lets the patient cancel by reply, sent inside the notice window, overrides the policy in the patient's mind. They were offered a cancel option and they took it. Charging a fee after that feels like a trap, and staff rarely enforce it.


A clinic contacted us this week about exactly this. Its reminder went out the day before the visit with "reply 1 to confirm or 2 to cancel." The patient replied 2, well inside the clinic's window, and the staff member who saw the reply cancelled the appointment without a fee. The owner's fix was to go through every reminder and remove the cancel option from any message that goes out after the deadline.


The rule is simple. The last message that offers a free cancellation or reschedule should arrive before the window closes. Reminders after that should ask only for confirmation and restate the fee. For a 48-hour window, that means a reminder at 72 hours with the reschedule option, and a confirm-only reminder at 24 hours. Wording matters too.[Two randomized trials published in PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0137306) found that reminders stating the cost of a missed appointment reduced missed visits more than a standard reminder.


## Deposits vs Card on File: Which Bookings Need Which


Use a card on file when you want the fee to be collectable, and a deposit when the slot is too expensive to risk. A card on file charges nothing up front, so it adds little friction to booking. A deposit is money already collected, which makes it the stronger commitment for long or high-ticket appointments.


The gap shows up with new patients from ads. A solo med spa owner told us on a sales call that she does not require a deposit and does not feel able to charge people who miss a visit, because most of her ad leads never put a card on file. Her substitute is a reminder cadence: a booking confirmation, then confirm requests two days, one day and two hours before the visit. She also wanted new ad leads handled differently from a patient of two years. That instinct is right. Another group told us they "run a lot on deposits" and wanted the card saved even when a campaign or an AI assistant makes the booking.


So decide by booking path as well as by service. An ad-driven online booking for a paid treatment should require a card or a deposit before the slot is held. A returning patient rebooked at checkout may need neither. If your software cannot apply different rules to online and staff-made bookings, write down which path the policy covers so staff are not guessing. Our post on[med spa online booking settings](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-online-booking-settings) covers the per-service rules that sit next to this one.


Watch for one more thing: patients who start a booking and never finish the deposit. The hold expires and nobody follows up. Decide who contacts those patients and when, because they came closer to booking than most leads on your list.


## Is a Med Spa Cancellation Fee Legal?


A cancellation or no-show fee is generally allowed when the patient was told about it in advance and agreed to it. The details depend on your state, so treat this section as orientation and have a local attorney review the final wording.


Two national sources set the baseline for medical practices. The American Medical Association's[Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 11.3.2](https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/fees-nonclinical-administrative-services) says physicians should clearly notify patients in advance of fees for nonclinical services, and it lists missed appointments, or appointments not cancelled in advance under the practice's published policy, among them. For clinics that see Medicare patients,[CMS guidance in MLN Matters MM5613](https://www.cms.gov/Outreach-and-Education/Medicare-Learning-Network-MLN/MLNMattersArticles/Downloads/MM5613.pdf) allows physicians and suppliers to charge beneficiaries for missed appointments, provided non-Medicare patients are charged the same amount. Medicare itself does not pay the charge.


Both sources point the same way: publish the policy, apply it to everyone, and tell the patient before they book. A fee the patient first hears about on the day it is charged is the one that draws a complaint.


## Med Spa Cancellation Policy Template (Copy and Edit)


The template below covers the six decisions from the first section. Replace the bracketed parts with your own numbers, and delete any clause you will not enforce. A clause you never apply weakens the ones you do.


> **Appointment changes.** We reserve your appointment time for you. To cancel or reschedule without a fee, contact us at least \[24/48\] hours before your appointment by \[phone, text or online link\].
>
>
> **Late cancellations.** Cancellations or reschedules made with less than \[24/48\] hours' notice are charged \[a fee of $X / X% of the booked service\]. This fee applies \[once per visit / to each booked service\].
>
>
> **No-shows.** If you miss your appointment without contacting us, you will be charged \[$X / X% of the booked service / your deposit\]. After \[two\] missed appointments we may require prepayment to book.
>
>
> **Late arrivals.** If you arrive more than \[10/15\] minutes late, we may need to shorten or reschedule your treatment, and the visit may be treated as a late cancellation.
>
>
> **Deposits and prepaid sessions.** Deposits are applied to your treatment and are refundable when you cancel on time. A prepaid package or membership session missed without notice is \[forfeited / subject to the fee above\].
>
>
> **Exceptions.** We waive fees for illness, emergencies, and any appointment we cancel or that your provider decides is not suitable to perform that day.
>
>
> **Agreement.** By booking, you confirm that you have read this policy and authorize us to charge the card on file for the fees described above.


Put the policy where the patient sees it before paying: on the booking page with a checkbox, in the confirmation message, and in the intake packet. Staff who book by phone should read the short version aloud and note that they did.


## Exceptions: Who Can Waive a Fee, and How to Record It


Decide in advance which fees the front desk can waive alone and which need a manager. Without that line, staff either waive everything to avoid conflict or refuse everything and escalate to the owner.


A workable split: the front desk can waive a first late cancellation for any patient and any fee tied to illness or a clinic-side cancellation. A manager approves waivers for repeat misses, for deposits on high-ticket appointments, and for any reversal of a recorded no-show. Clinical reasons are their own category. If a provider sees a cold sore, a sunburn or a new medication and declines to treat, that is the clinic's decision and no fee applies.


Record every waiver with a reason. Tell the patient, too. "We're waiving the fee this time" keeps the policy real. A silent waiver teaches the patient that the policy is not enforced. Scripts for these conversations belong in your[front desk training](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-front-desk-staffing-training) .


## When a Patient Disputes the Fee With Their Bank


When a patient disputes a cancellation charge with their card issuer, the outcome depends on what you can show about the policy and how the patient accepted it. Clinics have asked us what to do when a patient contests a no-show fee with their card issuer.


[Stripe's dispute documentation](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/categories) lists the evidence a merchant can submit for a cancelled-service claim: the language of the cancellation or refund policy as provided to the customer, an explanation of how and where the policy was provided before purchase, the reason the customer is not entitled to a refund, and any communication with the customer. Stripe also notes that for services booked in advance, such as reservations, evidence of a cancellation policy can be material.


That list tells you what to keep for every booking:


- The policy text as it appeared on the day the patient booked.
- A timestamped record of acceptance: the checkbox, the signed form, or the staff note from a phone booking.
- The reminder messages and the patient's replies.
- Notes from any conversation about the missed visit.


Keep clinical details out of the response. The dispute is about a booking and a policy, and the bank does not need to know what treatment was planned. For the wider picture on processors and disputes, see our guide to[Square and Stripe account freezes at med spas](https://decodahealth.com/blog/square-stripe-med-spa-account-freeze-guide) .


## What to Track After You Turn the Policy On


Track four numbers each month: late cancellations, no-shows, fees charged versus fees waived, and how many cancelled slots were rebooked. Together they tell you whether the policy changes behavior or only generates arguments.


Separate cancellations that rebook from those that do not. A patient who moves Tuesday to Thursday has cost you little, especially if the Tuesday slot was refilled. A patient who cancels and disappears is lost revenue. Owners have asked us for reports that split the two, because a single "cancellations" count hides the difference.


The waiver rate is the honest measure of enforcement. If most fees are waived, the policy exists on paper only, and patients will learn that quickly. A[med spa waitlist](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-waitlist) changes the math as well, since a slot that refills within the hour makes a strict fee harder to justify and a short notice window easier to offer.

## Final Thoughts on Your Med Spa Cancellation Policy


Write the policy around the cases that actually reach your front desk: the multi-service booking, the late arrival, the reminder that offers a way out, and the ad lead with no card saved. Set notice windows and fees by tier, say whether the fee is per visit or per service, and then book and cancel your own appointments to confirm the system does what the page says. ## Frequently Asked Questions


What is a standard med spa cancellation policy?


Most med spas ask for 24 hours of notice on short visits and 48 hours on long or high-ticket appointments such as laser and body contouring. Inside that window the patient pays a late-cancellation fee, and a no-show pays a higher one. The policy also needs a late-arrival rule, a list of exceptions, and a record that the patient agreed to it before booking.


How much should a med spa charge for a no-show?


Published vendor guides put the usual starting points at a flat fee or half the booked service for a late cancellation, and the full service price or the deposit for a no-show. Those figures are starting points and not survey data. Set your own from what the empty slot costs you, and decide whether the fee applies once per visit or once per service.


Is it legal for a med spa to charge a cancellation fee?


In general, yes, when the patient was told about the fee before booking and agreed to it. The American Medical Association's ethics guidance asks practices to notify patients in advance of fees for missed appointments, and Medicare lets physicians charge for missed appointments if every patient is charged the same. State consumer and contract rules vary, so have a local attorney review your wording.


Should a med spa charge the cancellation fee per appointment or per service?


Pick one and write it into the policy. A per-visit fee is easier for patients to understand and for staff to explain. A per-service fee can multiply when a patient books three treatments in one visit, which surprises both the patient and the front desk. Whichever you choose, check that your booking software charges it the same way your written policy describes it.


When does a late patient count as a no-show?


Set a grace period, commonly 10 to 15 minutes, after which the visit is shortened, rebooked or treated as a no-show at the provider's discretion. Then decide what happens when a patient arrives after being marked a no-show. If the provider can still see them, staff should be able to reverse the status and the fee, and record who approved it.


Do I need a deposit or is a card on file enough?


A card on file is enough for most short, mid-priced visits, because it makes the fee collectable without charging anything up front. Use a deposit for long or high-ticket appointments and for patients with a history of missed visits. New patients who book from an ad are the group least likely to have a card saved, so decide what that booking path requires.


Can a patient dispute a med spa no-show fee with their bank?


Yes. A patient can file a dispute with their card issuer, and the clinic then has to show its side. Keep the policy text the patient saw, a record of how and when they accepted it, the reminder messages, and any conversation about the missed visit. Card processors ask for exactly this evidence when a cancellation charge is challenged.
